newsitem.title: UK: U.S, European investors up Europe holdings - report.
newsitem.headline: U.S, European investors up Europe holdings - report.

text.p: European and U.S. investors increased their holdings of European stocks faster than the stocks of any other region during 1996, a report on global equity investment flows from fund data company Technimetrics said.
The report said European equities accounted for 56.1 percent of total U.S. investment abroad at the end of September, up from 51.7 percent at the end of 1995.
Non-domestic European stocks accounted for 45.9 percent of European international investment at the end of the third quarter, up from 45 percent in 1995.

The share of international investment in Asia-Pacific and Latin American stocks declined in the first three quarters of 1996 despite the fact that the value of equities held in each of these regions grew.

"While market performance certainly is a contributing factor, the clear impression remains that European companies are faring better at attracting international investment from the U.S. and Europe than their Latin American and Asia-Pacific competitors," the report said.
The report said the value of holdings in international stocks grew at a double digit pace among U.S. and European investors in the third quarter of 1996.
U.S. international holdings rose 12.9 percent, or $54.4 billion from the second quarter, while reported European holdings of non-domestic equities grew 12.3 pecrent, or $33.1 billion.
The report said the value of U.S. holdings in Europe rose 16.7 percent in the third quarter, with gains led by German stock holdings, which grew 26 percent in the quarter.
"Holdings in Europe's other major markets also grew, particularly in Dutch, Swiss and British equities," it said.
Canada's strong market performance continued to attract U.S. investment, with the value of U.S. holdings of Canadian stocks up 16.3 percent.
Ownership of Asia-Pacific stocks grew at a lesser rate, hindered by a fall of some $500 million in the value of U.S. holdings of Japanese equities.
European investors saw most of their gains in the third quarter come from holdings of North American and non-domestic European equities.
